messages.content: How far will a car travel in time 't' when launched with velocity 'v' at an angle 'theta'?

function.name: calculate_projectile_range
function.description: Calculate the range of a projectile launched at an angle with initial velocity, using the kinematic equation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

initial_velocity.description: The initial velocity at which projectile is launched. This is a float type value.

angle.description: The angle at which projectile is launched. This should be in degrees. This is a float type value.

time.description: The time in seconds after which the range is to be calculated. This is a float type value.

message.content:
**Short answer**

If you’re only interested in the **horizontal distance** covered while the vehicle moves under its own power (ignoring air‑drag or braking forces), simply multiply the forward component of the launch speed by the elapsed time:

\[
d_{\text{horiz}} \;=\; v\,\cos(\theta)\;\times\;t .
\]

That’s all there is—no gravity, no “projectile” effect comes into play because a car doesn’t follow ballistic trajectories once it has traction on the road.

---

### What if you really meant a *ballistic* trajectory?

Sometimes people phrase questions about cars in the same way they talk about projectiles.  
In that case you’d treat the car exactly like a thrown object subject to Earth’s gravitational acceleration \(g ≈ 9.81~\mathrm{m/s^{2}}\).

| Quantity | Formula |
|----------|---------|
| Flight time (until it lands back on level ground) | \(T_\text{flight}= \displaystyle \frac{2\,v\,\sin\!\theta}{g}\) |
| Horizontal distance (the classic “range”) | \(R = \displaystyle \frac{v^{2}}{g}\,\sin(2\theta)\) |

Now suppose you want the horizontal distance reached **after some arbitrary time \(t\)** (not necessarily equal to the full flight time):

```
if t ≤ T_flight:
    d_horiz(t) = v·cosθ · t          # still airborne – linear horizontal motion
else:
    d_horiz(t) = R                   # already landed – cannot move farther
```

So the piecewise rule is:

```math
d_{\text{horiz}}(t) =
   \begin{cases}
      v\,\cos(\theta)\;t , & t \leq \dfrac{2v\sin\theta}{g}\\[8pt]
      \dfrac{v^{2}}{g}\,\sin(2\theta), & t > \dfrac{2v\sin\theta}{g}
   \end{cases}
```

#### Why this works

During free fall the horizontal component of velocity stays constant (\(v_x = v\cos\theta\)). Therefore the horizontal position grows linearly with time until the moment the projectile hits the ground. After impact the horizontal coordinate stops changing (unless you give the car another push!).

---

### A quick sanity check

Let’s plug in numbers:

- Launch speed \(v = 20~\text{m/s}\)
- Launch angle \(\theta = 30^\circ\)

Compute the flight time first:

\[
T_\text{flight} = \frac{2\times20\times\sin30^\circ}{9.81}
                 = \frac{40\times0.5}{9.81}
                 \approx 2.04~\text{s}.
\]

Horizontal speed:

\[
v_x = 20\cos30^\circ \approx 17.32~\text{m/s}.
\]

Distance after \(t = 1~\text{s}\) (still airborne):

\[
d_{h}(1) = 17.32\times1 \approx 17.32~\text{m}.
\]

Full range (at \(t=T_\text{flight}\)):

\[
R = \frac{20^{2}}{9.81}\sin60^\circ 
  \approx \frac{400}{9.81}\times0.866
  \approx 35.3~\text{m}.
\]

Everything checks out!

---

### Bottom line

*For ordinary driving*: distance ≈ velocity × time (straight‑line assumption).  

*For a true projectile problem*: use the piecewise expression above, based on whether the chosen time lies inside or outside the flight interval.
